design_detail: Short report of a laboratory selectivity and sensitivity study of four brands of urine fentanyl immunoassay strips (BTNX Rapid Response, cut-off 20 ng/mL; Rapid Self Test FYL20, 20 ng/mL; Nal van Minden Drug-Screen FYL 10, 10 ng/mL; Hangzhou Alltest One Step FYL20 dipstick, 20 ng/mL) on single-compound solutions of reference compounds in Type 1 water, at one laboratory in Oslo. Fentanyl was tested at 10–1000 ng/mL; 28 fentanyl analogues at 100 and 1000 ng/mL, and at 10,000 ng/mL (carfentanil 4000 ng/mL) for compounds not clearly positive at 1000; three non-fentanyl synthetic opioids (U-47700, U-48800, U-50488), methadone and eight other drugs (amphetamine, cocaine, heroin, LSD, MDMA, methamphetamine, morphine, THC) at 100 and 1000 ng/mL. Fentanyl, carfentanil and remifentanil (1000 ng/mL) were also tested with heroin (50,000 ng/mL) or ascorbic acid (75 mg/mL), ascorbic acid alone at 0–75 mg/mL, and four analogues at 10 ng/mL alone and mixed (one brand). Strips were dipped for 13–20 s as the urine instructions state and graded by the authors on a four-level scale. Filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1): the units are prepared solutions, and the study is appraised with QUADAS-2 because strip readings are compared with known content, as in sc_green_2020; the reference is the known preparation, not a second analytical method. The online supplement (compound list and sources, procedural detail, supplementary figures) was not read.
can_establish: Which of 28 fentanyl analogues and 12 other drugs four brands of urine fentanyl strips reacted to, as pure single compounds in water at set concentrations read by the authors, how strongly detection depended on concentration and on the reading rule, and whether heroin, ascorbic acid or a mixture of low-level analogues changed the reading.
cannot_establish: How accurate the strips are on street drug samples prepared and read by people who check drugs, how often undetected analogues occur in any drug market, lot-to-lot or reader variation (no replicates reported), cross-reactivity with non-fentanyl drugs above 1000 ng/mL or with cutting agents other than ascorbic acid, or any effect on behaviour or overdose.

sample.recruitment: Not people or street samples: compounds bought from commercial distributors (see Table 1 and the supplement, not read) and dissolved in Type 1 water (Methods › Chemicals; Preparation of drug solutions, p. 2). n_total counts the 41 compounds tested (editors' count).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Analogues described as currently on the recreational drug market, among them the pharmaceutical fentanyls alfentanil, remifentanil and sufentanil, carfentanil, and the related compounds norcarfentanil and despropionyl-2-fluorofentanyl; the rule for choosing the panel is not stated.
sample.attrition: Not every compound was tested at every concentration: five analogues (alfentanil, despropionyl-2-fluorofentanyl, norcarfentanil, remifentanil, sufentanil) were not measured at 100 ng/mL but are counted as negative in that column's totals, and 10,000 ng/mL was tested only for compounds not clearly positive at 1000 ng/mL (editors' reading of Table 1, p. 2). Strip lots, replicates and the number of strips per condition are not reported in the main text.
sample.selection_effects: Pure single compounds in water at fixed concentrations are the conditions most favourable to clear readings and the least like street samples, which hold unknown amounts with mixtures and cutting agents. The analogue panel is not weighted by how often each compound occurs in any market, so the number of analogues detected says nothing about the share of real samples a strip would flag.

exposure.measurement: Index tests: four urine fentanyl strip brands, bought for the study, dipped for 13–20 s per the makers' urine instructions (Methods › Fentanyl test strips; Fentanyl test strip experiments, p. 2). Reading: the makers' instructions call a test negative whenever a test band appears, whatever its intensity (Results › Interpretation of test results; Fig. 1A, p. 3). After seeing concentration-dependent bands, the authors graded ‘++’ clearly positive (no test band), ‘+’ positive (barely visible test band), ‘(+)’ weak positive or ambiguous (faint test band) and ‘−’ negative (solid test band), and counted ++ and + as positive (p. 3).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (no dosing). Test concentrations: fentanyl 10–1000 ng/mL; analogues 100, 1000 and 10,000 ng/mL, carfentanil 4000 ng/mL, chosen from a cited estimate (Casale et al., 2017) that 20 μg of carfentanil, about 4000 ng/mL in 5 mL, is potentially life-threatening; other drugs 100 and 1000 ng/mL; heroin 50,000 ng/mL; ascorbic acid 0–75 mg/mL, included because acids are used when heroin base is prepared for injection (cited study); four-analogue mixture at 10 ng/mL each (Preparation of drug solutions, p. 2).
exposure.polysubstance: Single compounds, except fentanyl, carfentanil and remifentanil each with heroin or with ascorbic acid, and a mixture of acetyl-, acryl-, furanyl- and butyrfentanyl at 10 ng/mL each tested with Nal van Minden only. No cutting agents other than ascorbic acid and no stimulant–fentanyl mixtures.

comparison.controls: Reference: the known content of each prepared solution; Type 1 water as negative control and fentanyl 1000 ng/mL as positive control (Fig. 1B, p. 3). No analytical check of the prepared concentrations is reported in the main text.
comparison.matching: Not applicable; all four brands were tested on the same solutions.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to solutions. Not reported in the main text: strip lots and expiry dates, number of replicates, who read the strips and whether readers knew the content, reading time, and agreement between readers.

outcomes.instruments: Visual grading of each strip on the authors' four-level scale; for each brand and concentration, the number of the 28 analogues graded positive (++ or +), weak or ambiguous, and negative (Table 1, p. 2); results for the other drugs and for the heroin, ascorbic acid and mixture experiments in the text and Figs. 1–2.
outcomes.validity_norms: The makers' cut-offs (10 or 20 ng/mL) refer to urine; use on drug solutions is off-label. The authors' grading departs from the makers' reading rule, and no reliability between readers or runs is reported.
outcomes.operationalization: Positive = no test band or a barely visible one (++ or +); faint band = weak positive or ambiguous; solid band = negative. The 10,000 ng/mL totals are cumulative over 1000 and 10,000 ng/mL (Table 1 note a).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not reported; nothing in the main text suggests that readers were blind to the solutions.

analysis.effect_sizes: No statistics; counts only (Table 1, p. 2). By the authors' counting rule (++ or + positive), analogues detected at 100 ng/mL: Rapid Response 5, Rapid Self Test 5, One Step 12, Nal van Minden 9 (of the 23 actually measured, editors' count; the printed totals count the 5 unmeasured as negative); at 1000 ng/mL 21, 19, 15 and 22 of 28; cumulative to 10,000 ng/mL 24, 24, 21 and 24 of 28. Editors' recount by the makers' rule as the paper describes it (only ++, no test band, positive): at 100 ng/mL 1, 2, 11 and 4 of 23; at 1000 ng/mL 18, 16, 14 and 20 of 28; cumulative 20, 20, 19 and 21 of 28; fentanyl itself at 100 ng/mL was + (a barely visible band) on Rapid Response and Rapid Self Test. Editors' recount reading faint bands as presence, as the authors recommend: 13, 9, 14 and 15 of 23 at 100 ng/mL; cumulative 25, 25, 21 and 25 of 28. Editors' calculation (Wilson 95% CI, treating the panel as if it were sampled, which it is not): 24/28 = 85.7% (68.5–94.3%); 21/28 = 75.0% (56.6–87.3%). No positive results from the 12 non-fentanyl drugs at 100 and 1000 ng/mL on any brand; One Step positive with ascorbic acid alone at 10, 25 and 75 mg/mL, not at 1.5 mg/mL. Fentanyl itself, in the descending series pictured for two brands (Fig. 1C, p. 3): lowest positive reading 50 ng/mL (Rapid Response) and 25 ng/mL (One Step) by the authors' rule, 100 and 50 ng/mL by the makers' rule.
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned.
analysis.selective_reporting: The additive-mixture result is reported for one brand only and generalized to all brands by expectation; heroin and ascorbic acid were tested with three compounds at one concentration; results for the non-fentanyl drugs are given in one sentence without a table; procedural detail and supplementary figures are in the online supplement (not read).
analysis.power: Not applicable. No replicates are reported, so the reproducibility of single cells, especially borderline + and (+) readings, is unknown.

interpretation_gap.results_show: All four brands reacted to fentanyl, and to most of the 28 analogues at 1000 ng/mL or more (21–24 of 28 by the authors' counting rule), but to far fewer at 100 ng/mL (5–12 of the 23 measured, editors' count). No brand reacted to alfentanil, despropionyl-2-fluorofentanyl or norcarfentanil; carfentanil read positive on no brand at 1000 ng/mL (a faint test band, weak or ambiguous, on three brands; a solid band, negative, on One Step) and was clearly positive at 4000 ng/mL on three brands, never on One Step. Detection depended on concentration and on how faint bands are read: by the makers' rule the counts are lower. No reactions to 12 non-fentanyl drugs at up to 1000 ng/mL; ascorbic acid at 10 mg/mL or more gave false positives on One Step; heroin changed nothing.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that “All test strips detected fentanyl as well as 21–24 of the 28 fentanyl analogues” (p. 1) without saying that these counts use 1000–10,000 ng/mL and the authors' own reading of barely visible bands as positive; at 100 ng/mL detection was 5–12 of the 23 measured (editors' count). The Conclusion's “detecting the vast majority of the fentanyl analogues present on the recreational drug market” (p. 4) generalizes from a panel not weighted by market occurrence. The recommendation to read faint bands as presence was not tested for its effect on false positives, and the recommendation to test injection solutions without further dilution (p. 4) is not reconciled with the authors' own finding that ascorbic acid, which they included to model injection solutions, gave false positives on One Step. The abstract's caution that the strips are no panacea, because some analogues are missed, is supported.

timeline.event: Casale et al. (2017): analysis of illicit carfentanil, cited for the estimate that 20 μg can be life-threatening, which set the 4000 ng/mL test concentration; not read.
McGowan et al. (2018), cited as background on whether enough is known to promote fentanyl self-testing outside supervised settings; not read.

Green et al. (2020): BTNX strips detected fentanyl in 104 of 106 police-seized samples and were positive in all four exploratory samples containing acetyl fentanyl or furanyl fentanyl (card sc_green_2020), consistent with detection of these analogues here at 1000 ng/mL; that study also recorded strip positives in seized samples negative for fentanyl by GC/MS.

Lockwood et al. (2021): solutions of seized methamphetamine and MDMA and of retail diphenhydramine gave false positives on BTNX Rapid Response strips at about 1–2.5 mg/mL of material, 1000 to 2500 times the 1000 ng/mL ceiling tested here. Read in this round (card sc_lockwood_2021).

Sisco et al. (2024b) cite this study among laboratory studies of strip false positives and analogue detection; read in this round (card sc_sisco_2024b), though it did not test fentanyl-strip cross-reactivity.

Halifax et al. (2024): five lots of BTNX Rapid Response strips detected 11 of 13 fentanyl analogues, never alfentanil, and carfentanil on every lot but on two lots obtained in 2021 only from 10 000 ng/mL; pure d-methamphetamine and MDMA gave false positives at mg/mL concentrations. Read in this round (card sc_halifax_2024).

replication.where_it_stands: Detection of acetyl and furanyl fentanyl is consistent with the seized-sample study (Green et al., 2020). Five lots of the BTNX strip in another laboratory also detected most of a 13-analogue panel, never alfentanil, and carfentanil on every lot but on two newer lots only from 10 000 ng/mL (Halifax et al., 2024), which agrees with the carfentanil gap here. Methamphetamine and MDMA, negative here at up to 1000 ng/mL, gave false positives at mg/mL concentrations in two other laboratories (Lockwood et al., 2021; Halifax et al., 2024), so the studies do not conflict, but this study cannot exclude cross-reactivity at higher concentrations. The One Step ascorbic acid artefact has no independent check among the papers read.

funding.funder: No funding statement beyond the Acknowledgments: M.H. Baumann is funded by the Intramural Research Program of the National Institute on Drug Abuse, National Institutes of Health (p. 5). The strips were purchased for the study (p. 2).
funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare no conflicts of interest related to the study (Declarations of Interests, p. 5).
funding.affiliations_note: Authors from the Section for Drug Abuse Research, Department of Forensic Sciences, Oslo University Hospital, the University of Oslo (Department of Chemistry; Institute of Basic Medical Sciences) and the Designer Drug Research Unit of the NIDA Intramural Research Program, Baltimore. No link to a strip maker is declared. Open access under a CC BY licence. A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Replicate testing of several lots of each brand, read blind by trained and untrained readers under both the makers' and the authors' reading rules, on street samples and on solutions prepared as they are in drug-checking practice (with mixtures, cutting agents, acids and stimulants at realistic concentrations), against quantitative LC-MS/MS, with analogues weighted by how often they appear in current drug-checking data.

preclinical.species_strain_sex: Not applicable (prepared drug solutions; no animals or cells).
preclinical.dose_route_schedule: Not applicable (no dosing); test concentrations as in the exposure fields.
preclinical.resembles_human_use: Partly: the strips and the makers' urine instructions are those used in drug checking, but the samples were pure single compounds of known concentration in laboratory water, read by laboratory scientists, whereas street samples contain unknown amounts with mixtures and cutting agents; the authors note that the dilution described in community guidance would give lower concentrations than an injection solution (Discussion, 3rd paragraph, p. 4).

domains.note: Prepared single-compound solutions of reference materials at fixed concentrations, not street samples; a chosen analogue panel; negatives limited to 12 drugs at up to 1000 ng/mL plus ascorbic acid. Known-positive and known-negative solutions are a case-control-like design that favours clear results; applicability to drug checking is low.

Readers are not described and probably knew the content; the four-level grading was devised after seeing concentration-dependent results, and its threshold (++ or +) differs from the makers' rule; lots, replicates and reading time are not reported in the main text; Table 1 and Fig. 1C grade the same result (Rapid Response, fentanyl 100 ng/mL) differently (+ v ++).
Content known by preparation from commercial reference compounds; the concentrations are not reported as verified, a minor concern.

Not every compound was tested at every concentration: five analogues not measured at 100 ng/mL are counted as negative; 10,000 ng/mL only for compounds not clearly positive at 1000; carfentanil's 4000 ng/mL result sits in the 10,000 column; the co-presence experiments used three compounds and the mixture experiment one brand.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: QUADAS-2 is used because strip readings are compared with known content (METHODS §5.3, diagnostic accuracy); the design is filed as test-accuracy (METHODS §5.3, version 0.3.1). The overall judgment follows the worst domains (artificial samples; unblinded, post hoc grading with a non-standard threshold). These problems mostly favour detection, so the study is better evidence of what the strips miss (three analogues entirely, carfentanil below 4000 ng/mL on the authors' counting rule, most analogues at 100 ng/mL) than of how often they would flag analogues in real samples. Citable for: each brand's reactions to each of the 28 analogues at the concentrations tested, under a stated reading rule; no reaction to alfentanil, despropionyl-2-fluorofentanyl or norcarfentanil; strong dependence on concentration and on the reading rule; no reaction to 12 non-fentanyl drugs at up to 1000 ng/mL; false positives with ascorbic acid on One Step; no effect of heroin. Not citable for: accuracy on street samples or when people test, the share of real samples with undetected analogues, other lots or brands, or effects on behaviour or overdose.

key_findings.finding: Four urine fentanyl strip brands were bought and tested: BTNX Rapid Response (cut-off 20 ng/mL), Rapid Self Test FYL20 (20 ng/mL), Nal van Minden Drug-Screen FYL 10 (10 ng/mL) and Hangzhou Alltest One Step FYL20 (20 ng/mL), dipped for 13–20 s in single-compound solutions in Type 1 water: 28 analogues at 100 and 1000 ng/mL and, where needed, 10,000 ng/mL (carfentanil 4000 ng/mL); non-fentanyl drugs at 100 and 1000 ng/mL.
key_findings.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Methods › Fentanyl test strips; Preparation of drug solutions for fentanyl test strip experiments; Fentanyl test strip experiments

key_findings.finding: The makers' instructions call a strip negative whenever two bands appear, however faint the test band (Fig. 1A). Fentanyl at 1000 ng/mL and water gave clear positive and negative results on all brands, but fentanyl at 10–250 ng/mL gave concentration-dependent bands (Fig. 1C labels: Rapid Response ++ at 250 and 100, + at 50, (+) at 25, − at 10; One Step ++ at 250 to 50, + at 25, (+) at 10). The authors therefore graded ++, +, (+) and − and counted ++ and + as positive.
key_findings.locator: Results › Interpretation of test results, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1
key_findings.note: Table 1 grades Rapid Response with fentanyl at 100 ng/mL as +, Fig. 1C as ++.

key_findings.finding: All brands were positive for fentanyl at 100 and 1000 ng/mL: + on Rapid Response and Rapid Self Test at 100 ng/mL, ++ on One Step and Nal van Minden; ++ on all at 1000 ng/mL.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (Fentanyl row); Results › Selectivity of fentanyl test strips, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: A + is a barely visible test band, which the makers' rule as described would read as negative (editors' note).

key_findings.finding: Cumulative over 1000 and 10,000 ng/mL, Rapid Response, Rapid Self Test and Nal van Minden were positive for 24 of 28 analogues, all except alfentanil, despropionyl-2-fluorofentanyl, norcarfentanil and remifentanil (the last weak or ambiguous at 10,000 ng/mL); One Step for 21, missing also benzodioxolefentanyl, carfentanil and sufentanil.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (summary rows); Results › Selectivity of fentanyl test strips, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: At 1000 ng/mL, analogues positive: Rapid Response 21, Rapid Self Test 19, One Step 15 and Nal van Minden 22 of 28 (weak or ambiguous 2, 4, 2 and 1).

At 100 ng/mL (5–10 times the cut-offs), analogues positive: One Step 12, Nal van Minden 9, Rapid Response 5 and Rapid Self Test 5 (weak or ambiguous 2, 6, 8 and 4). Only 4-fluoroisobutyrfentanyl, acetylfentanyl, acrylfentanyl and methoxyacetylfentanyl were positive at 100 ng/mL on all four brands (editors' reading of Table 1).
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (summary rows); Results › Sensitivity of fentanyl test strips, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Only 23 analogues were measured at 100 ng/mL; the printed negative counts (Rapid Response 15, Rapid Self Test 19, One Step 14, Nal van Minden 13) include the five not measured (editors' count).

key_findings.finding: No brand was positive (++ or +) for carfentanil at 1000 ng/mL: Rapid Response, Rapid Self Test and Nal van Minden gave a weak or ambiguous band and One Step was negative. The first three were clearly positive at 4000 ng/mL, the concentration the authors equate with a potentially life-threatening 20 μg in 5 mL; One Step was negative at every concentration.
key_findings.locator: Table 1 (Carfentanil row and note b); Results › Sensitivity of fentanyl test strips, 2nd paragraph
key_findings.note: Under the authors' own recommendation to read faint bands as presence, the three weak bands at 1000 ng/mL would count as detections (editors' note).

key_findings.finding: Analogues positive only at the highest concentration (editors' reading of Table 1): 4-methoxybutyrfentanyl, carfentanil and sufentanil on Rapid Response; these plus 4-fluorocyclopropylbenzylfentanyl and furanylbenzylfentanyl on Rapid Self Test; carfentanil and sufentanil on Nal van Minden; 2-fluorofentanyl, 3-methylcrotonylfentanyl, 4-methoxybutyrfentanyl, cis-3-methylfentanyl, ocfentanil and valerylfentanyl on One Step.
All brands were negative for U-47700, U-48800, U-50488, methadone, amphetamine, cocaine, heroin, LSD, MDMA, methamphetamine, morphine and THC, each tested at 100 and 1000 ng/mL.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Preparation of drug solutions for fentanyl test strip experiments; Results › Selectivity of fentanyl test strips, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: With ascorbic acid, strips at 25 mg/mL or more looked smeared and pale pink but read as before, except that One Step turned clearly positive for carfentanil and remifentanil; ascorbic acid alone (tested at 0, 1.5, 10, 25 and 75 mg/mL) gave false positives on One Step at 10 mg/mL and above, not at 1.5 mg/mL, and none on the other brands. Heroin (50,000 ng/mL) changed no result.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Preparation of drug solutions for fentanyl test strip experiments (p. 2); Results › The effect of ascorbic acid and heroin on test results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Fig. 2 (p. 4)
key_findings.note: Fig. 2 shows Rapid Response and One Step only; the legend states that the other two brands were unaffected.

key_findings.finding: Acetyl-, acryl-, furanyl- and butyrfentanyl at 10 ng/mL were each negative or weak alone but positive as a mixture (each 10 ng/mL); tested with Nal van Minden only, and expected by the authors to hold for all brands.
key_findings.locator: Results › Additive effect of fentanyl analogues for test strip results, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: The authors depart from the makers' rule, arguing that a faint test band should be read as indicating fentanyls because results were so concentration dependent, and recommend against further dilution of injection solutions before testing, since the dilution described by web stores and harm-reduction organizations would lower concentrations and the chance of detecting carfentanil.

The authors conclude that the strips detect the vast majority of analogues on the market but are highly concentration dependent, are unaffected by heroin, give false positives with ascorbic acid on one brand and detect carfentanil poorly; useful for harm reduction with information on their limits, but no panacea.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1's totals at 100 ng/mL count as negative five analogues that were not measured at that concentration (alfentanil, despropionyl-2-fluorofentanyl, norcarfentanil, remifentanil, sufentanil), and the text says all strips were tested with analogue solutions at 100 ng/mL.
reporting_issues.consequence: Denominators at 100 ng/mL are 23 measured analogues, not 28; treating compounds negative at 1000 ng/mL as negative at 100 is reasonable but unstated.

reporting_issues.issue: The 10,000 ng/mL totals are cumulative over 1000 and 10,000 ng/mL (Table 1 note a), and carfentanil's entry in that column was measured at 4000 ng/mL; the Discussion speaks of 4000–10,000 ng/mL for carfentanil, though no 10,000 ng/mL carfentanil test is described.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the 21–24 of 28 as detection at 1000 ng/mL or above, and carfentanil as tested up to 4000 ng/mL.

reporting_issues.issue: Fig. 1C grades Rapid Response with fentanyl at 100 ng/mL as ++, Table 1 as +.
reporting_issues.consequence: Readings of borderline bands vary between runs or readers; with no replicates reported, single + or (+) cells are uncertain.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract's counts (21–24 of 28) rest on the authors' reading of barely visible test bands as positive, contrary to the makers' rule the paper describes; by editors' recount under the makers' rule the cumulative counts are 19–21 of 28 and, at 100 ng/mL, 1–11 of 23.
reporting_issues.consequence: Claims should state the reading rule and concentration with any detection count.

reporting_issues.issue: The mixture experiment was done with one brand, and the main-text Fig. 2 shows two of the four brands; the mixture and co-presence results refer to supplementary figures. The statement that the additive effect is general is an expectation, not a result.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the mixture result for Nal van Minden only.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusion recommends testing injection solutions without further dilution, but the paper's own data show One Step false positives with ascorbic acid, which the authors included to model injection solutions, at 10 mg/mL and above.
reporting_issues.consequence: The recommendation is not reconciled with the ascorbic acid finding and should not be cited as tested.
